content.summary_of_the_paper: This work studies the problem of visual prompting, i.e., adapting large-scale pre-trained models by adding learnable perturbation to images at pixel level. Although previous visual prompting works bridges adversarial attack and visual prompt, the gap between visual prompting and linear probe is significant. This work tackled this challenge by (1) integrating adversarial attack tools, i.e., gradient normalization and input diversity, and (2) shrinking the original image into a smaller size and then padding it with learnable parameters back to the original size. Experiments are conducted across 17 datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

\+ The research problem of visual prompting is recent and not fully explored.

\+ The proposed framework is simple but effective. It outperforms VP and VPT, and even outperforms linear probe on most of the datasets according to Table 1.

\+ Experiments are conducted on 12 datasets to show the effectiveness, which is comprehensive.

\+ The writing quality of this paper is good. 

Weaknesses & Questions

\- Although the framework is simple but effective, the tools are existing methods in adversarial attack. The novelty of these tools is not strong. There lack comprehensive theoretical analysis and motivation why these tools help. Are there other tools in adversarial attack that are not helpful in visual prompt? The lack of answers to these questions makes the method less novel, and the contributions of this paper mainly comes from experimental implementation.

\- The compared baselines include (zero-shot) Text Prompt, VP, VPT, Linear Prob, and Fully fine-tuning. Recent works also proposed to fine-tune text prompt. It would be great if this type of baseline models [1, 2] can be compared. If not, it would be interesting to know the reason why not comparing them. It is acceptable if the comparison with [1, 2] is not fair, but it is still important to explain the reasons.

\- It is not clear enough the different of settings in Tables 1 and 2. What is the setting of "arbitrary mapping"?

\- Text size in Tables 1-5 is too small.

References

[1] Learning to Prompt for Vision-Language Models. IJCV.

[2] Conditional Prompt Learning for Vision-Language Models. CVPR 2022.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the problem of visual prompting at the pixel level. Based on the well-known technical similarity between generating adversarial images and generating visual prompts, the authors propose to adopt existing techniques in the adversarial image literature to improve visual prompting. Specifically, the authors adopt two techniques: input diversity, which is originally used for improving the transferability of adversarial images, and gradient normalization, which is originally used to limit the perturbation size. The results show that the new method outperforms two baseline visual prompting methods and is comparable to Linear Probe, which instead requires model parameter tuning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Migrating simple, existing techniques from a similar task is a good practice before inventing new (complex) methods.
2. The experiments are extensive and diverse, involving 12 classical, 3 out-of-distribution, and 2 corruption classification datasets. Two prompting baselines, LP (Linear Probe), and FT (Fully fine-tuning) are compared.
3. Ablation studies on the two main components, input diversity, and gradient normalization, are carried out.

Weaknesses:
1. Several contributions are over-claimed. First, padding the original images without covering their content has also been adopted in the original Adversarial reprogramming paper (Elsayed et al., 2018) but not a novel proposal of this submission. Second, the impact of the similarity between pre-trained classes and downstream classes on the performance has also been explored in the VP paper (see their section 6.3).

2. The general motivation of “bridging adversarial attack and visual prompt” does not seem to hold. As far as the reviewer knows, the gradient normalization in adversarial attacks is solely used for imposing the perturbation bounds instead of improving the attack performance. The authors also do not provide any direct evidence or references showing that gradient normalization helps improve the attack performance. In fact, normalized gradient descent is a well-known trick [A] for stabilizing the gradient update in machine learning but is not relevant to adversarial attacks.
In a similar sense, the input diversity design in this submission (using RandomHorizontalFlip and advanced augmentations) is also different from those commonly used in the adversarial transferability literature, e.g., random resizing&padding [Xie et al. 2019], translation [B], and pixel scaling [C].
In sum, the two main components are just common techniques for improving machining learning optimization but not specifically relevant to adversarial attacks. 

3. The main assumption that “additive visual prompt on the original image may cover up the original image information. Thus, it becomes a new burden to improve classification performance further” is not explicitly validated. The authors separate the visual prompt and image by simply shrinking the original image into a smaller size and then padding it with the visual prompts. In this way, it is not clear whether the performance gain is from the shrinking operation or the separation. In order to validate the assumption, it is necessary to conduct experiments by controlling the shrinking.

4. In Section 3.3., the authors motivate the idea of using adversarial attack techniques to help visual prompting by stating that adversarial attacks minimize the probability w.r.t. the true label while visual prompting maximizes it. However, it is well-known that targeted adversarial attacks actually also maximize the probability. For this reason, the reviewer is wondering if some technique [D] that is specifically designed for improving the transferability of targeted adversarial attacks can actually yield better performance.

5. It is not fair to say that EVP only needs to train only 0.04% of parameters compared to the FT. As can be seen from Table 1, EVP outperforms LP but is still worse than FT. It would make more sense to determine the number of fine-tuned parameters that can achieve exactly the same performance as EVP. This could be done by gradually adding more parameters for fine-tuning ranging from the last layer (LP) to all layers (FT). The reviewer would expect that to achieve the same performance as EVP, the fine-tuning would need far fewer parameters compared to FT.

6. How are 5 out of the 12 datasets selected for the few-shot experiments reported in Figure 4? Based on the previous results, it seems that the best 5 datasets are selected. This is not a fair comparison. Please test all 12 datasets.

7. The ablation study should also show the results of using only one of the two components, compared to the baseline. The current results just report the results when both are used.

8. The method of leveraging class similarity information discussed in Section 4.3 is a general technique but not specially limited to EVP. To better validate its effectiveness, the authors should test all three prompting methods, i.e., VP, VPT, and EVP, with and without leveraging class similarity. 

[A] Ryan Murray, Brian Swenson, Soummya Kar. Revisiting Normalized Gradient Descent: Fast Evasion of Saddle Points. arXiv 2017.

[B] Yinpeng Dong, Tianyu Pang, Hang Su, Jun Zhu. Evading Defenses to Transferable Adversarial Examples by Translation-Invariant Attacks. CVPR 2019.

[C] Jiadong Lin, Chuanbiao Song, Kun He, Liwei Wang, John E. Hopcroft. Nesterov Accelerated Gradient and Scale Invariance for Adversarial Attacks. ICLR 2020.

[D] Zhengyu Zhao, Zhuoran Liu, Martha Larson. On Success and Simplicity: A Second Look at Transferable Targeted Attacks. NeurIPS 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing is generally satisfying, but the contributions of this paper are very limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: Considering the limited novelty and the lack of supportive experiments, as listed in the above weaknesses, I vote for rejecting the paper at this moment.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Driven by the observed gaps between linear probe and visual prompting, this paper enhances the vanilla visual prompting via integrating the existing techniques designed for adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments show that the proposed visual prompting scheme outperforms previous visual prompt designs and also surpasses the accuracy of linear probe.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

1. As also mentioned the authors, it is not clear whether visual prompting is a preferable alternative as compared to simple linear probe. The proposed method can shed light on the answer to this question, which can be insightful for the community.

2. The proposed method is validated by extensive experiments in terms of accuracy and robustness across standard learning/few-shot learning.

**Weakness**

1. My major concern for this paper is the limited novelty. Empowering new applications with old ideas can be solid contributions, while the main issue is that only two simple techniques are migrated to visual prompting and it is not clear whether the effectiveness of the two techniques originates from the connections between visual prompting and adversarial attacks. For example, data augmentation can generally reduce overfitting and improve finetuning accuracy, and gradient normalization naturally adjusts the learning rate, which can also explain the effectiveness in visual prompting. 

2. It is not clear whether the insight about the correlation between visual prompting and adversarial attacks is generalizable. Examining or analyzing the  effectiveness of more techniques from the adversarial field in visual prompting to provide a more general insight can greatly strengthen the contributions of this paper.

3. For the benchmark in Fig.3 (a), the proposed EVP outperforms linear probe by a large margin on SVHN and thus achieves a higher averaged accuracy. A natural question is when will EVP become a better choice than linear probe for users' perspective?

4. In addition to classifications tasks, evaluating visual prompting on more downstream tasks (e.g., object detection and segmentation) will greatly strengthen the experiment, which validates whether visual prompting can serve as a general finetuning scheme.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper shows good clarity in the presentation while the novelty is somewhat limited as elaborated in the weakness section. The reproducibility is not clear as no code or statement is provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: My major concerns are the limited novelty and the uncertainty about the generality of the claimed insights. I tend to rank this paper as marginally below the acceptance threshold and I'm willing to adjust my scores if my concerns are properly addressed.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper experiments the pixel-level visual prompt with data augmentations and gradient normalization, borrowed from adversarial training. The experimental results show improvement over linear probing and visual prompt tuning on almost all datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength 

This paper provides good insights on bridging adversarial learning and pixel-level visual prompt.

Weakness

The connection between pixel-level visual prompt and adversarial learning are very limited and the exploration is not enough to provide justification of adversarial learning strategies would be helpful for visual prompting.

The experiment results are not very convincing, especially on results of ResNets as shown in Table 2, where the proposed method performs less compared with both linear probing and full fine-tuning. Besides, the total parameters of visual prompting is not provided to justify its parameter efficiency.

Experiment setup and hyperparameters is not provided. The reason I think this part should be provided in detail is regarding the gradient normalization in Eq. 2. The normalization of gradient is equivalent to scale the learning rate for visual prompt (since only pixel-level prompt and linear head are trainable), but neither justification nor experiments on this are provided. This also weaken the core statement made in this work on bridging adversarial training and visual prompting.

The ablation on data augmentation is data sensitive and domain sensitive. Doing ablation only on CIFAR cannot provide enough verification of input diversity. As in VTAB-1k, different datasets usually require different types of augmentations, especially for those with large domain shift.
